title: Visual Arts and Generative Illustration
answer: Prompt architecture, concept art, vector assets, inpainting and colour: the still image made with diffusion models.

children.name: Prompt Architecture and Style Replication
children.blurb: Prompt Architecture and Style Replication covers the practice of writing and structuring text prompts so that an image model reproduces a chosen visual style, whether that style belongs to a named artist, a studio house look, a period, or the illustrator's own earlier work.

children.name: Concept Art and World-Building
children.blurb: Concept art and world-building cover the visual development work that happens before a film, game, or series is produced: characters, creatures, environments, props, vehicles, and the rules that hold a fictional setting together.

children.name: Vector Graphics and Interface Assets
children.blurb: Vector graphics and interface assets cover the artwork that stays sharp at any size and the small pieces that make software usable: icons, logos, buttons, illustration systems, and design tokens.

children.name: Inpainting and Canvas Expansion
children.blurb: Inpainting is the practice of regenerating a selected region of an existing image while leaving the rest untouched, and canvas expansion, sometimes called outpainting, extends an image beyond its original borders.

children.name: Algorithmic Colour Grading
children.blurb: Algorithmic colour grading covers the use of software, including machine learning models, to adjust the colour, contrast, tone and mood of moving or still images.

sections.body: This section covers the still image made with diffusion models, the kind of picture that is generated, edited and finished inside a prompt box and a canvas rather than a camera or a drawing tablet. In practice, artists now use these systems to draft concept art, produce vector assets for interfaces, extend or repair existing images, and push colour in directions that would take hours by hand. The work is less about typing a magic phrase and more about building a prompt the way a photographer builds a shot, with subject, lens, light and reference all specified. Style replication sits at the centre of it, because a model can imitate a named artist or a house style closely enough that the output is usable as a starting point. What the field is actually doing is compressing the early stages of visual development, not replacing the later ones.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The technology is genuinely good at producing a plausible single image from a text description, and it is genuinely good at filling a masked region or extending a canvas outward. It is weaker at consistency across a set, at precise spatial control, and at anything requiring exact typography or a specific brand mark. Vector output remains the least settled area, because diffusion models work in pixels and clean scalable paths still need conversion or manual redrawing. Colour grading with these tools is fast but often drifts, and matching a reference palette across a sequence takes iteration. The honest limit is that the model has no understanding of intent, so the artist carries the judgement, the selection and the correction. Legal questions around training data and style imitation are unresolved, and this section describes the practice rather than settling them.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the pipeline from idea to finished asset. Prompt Architecture and Style Replication is the entry point, covering how a prompt is structured and how a named style is approximated or blended. Concept Art and World-Building takes that further into sets of images that share a world, a character or a mood, which is where consistency problems show up most clearly. Vector Graphics and Interface Assets deals with the harder conversion from generated pixels to clean paths and usable components. Inpainting and Canvas Expansion covers repair and extension, the editing moves that turn a single generation into a workable composition. Algorithmic Colour Grading closes the sequence by treating palette and tone as something that can be directed, matched and corrected after the image exists. Read together, they describe a workflow rather than five separate tricks.
